If I roll a 20 sided die and am trying to hit 4 numbers I've chosen, are my odds of success higher if I pick the same four numbers (1,2,3,4) vs randomly choosing 4 each roll?

If randomly choosing increases possible success rate does it also increase possible failure rate?

Assuming rolls are independant, with an equal chance for each number, then it doesn't matter either way. May as well use 1-4 or 17-20 just to make it easier to tell at a glance if you succeeded or not.

On a perfectly unbiased die, the numbers shouldn't matter and the probability should be the same. However, there are always going to be minor imperfections in mass produced goods that slightly favour an orientation based on slightly uneven weight distribution.

;-)

We've discussed this very thing, more or less, a few times. We have a resident expert in dice and probability.

Paging @VIP740 - who has been poking at this topic for a while now. I'll stand aside and encourage others to answer.

LOL! I'm not sure I'd count as an expert, actually when I get through some of the computer stuff, I'm going to have to review calculus and go back over Jaynes more thoroughly.

I'm going to agree with everyone else here and say it shouldn't matter if the dice are unbiased. If the dice are biased (which real dice probably are) it's possible for some patterns to be favored over others.

If you're the one throwing it and you know the bias, that will help you get what you want. If you don't know the bias, randomizing the numbers you pick (with something other than dice?) would be like removing the bias, so you probably wouldn't do the worst possible, but you wouldn't have as much of a chance of doing the best possible either; so that would be a low risk low reward strategy. Picking the same numbers repeatedly would be the high risk high reward rout; but either way it probably wouldn't make much difference.

See? Told 'em you were the expert. Assuming the die is unbiased, the odds will remain exactly the same.

And, from a physics point of view, the dice will have some bias. So, you're correct again!

You're saying random numbers is the low risk, low reward option and (1-4) is the high risk, high reward?

Could you expand on that at all?

Let's say the numbers are weighted, but you don't know how. It's possible 1 is the most likely and as the numbers go higher the get less likely until 20 is the leas likely. If that were the case then 1, 2, 3, and 4 would give you the best odds. But the opposite could just as easily be true. 20 could be the most likely, then 19, with the least likely being 4, 3, 2, and 1. So if you play the same numbers repeatedly, that could be the luckiest strategy, the unluckiest, or anything in between. This strategy might be appropriate if you're losing or behind, thinking you don't have much to lose. I suppose if you were very observant you could switch your strategy during the game if your strategy seemed bad; you'd have to be pretty good at keeping track of the numbers to do that though, and the difference in odds would probably be near impossible to detect.

If you're not going to pick the same numbers every time, then you won't be repeating the best or worst guesses over and over. You'll sometimes choose the luckiest numbers, and sometimes the unluckiest, so things will probably balance out. This strategy would be appropriate if you're ahead, and figure you have more to lose than you have to gain.

The fewer throws you have to play the less difference it will make, and unless there's a chance the dice are rigged, it probably won't make much difference anyway. You could choose your lucky numbers and win thinking they were the best, when actually, they were the worst.
